doc.title: Lanny Morgan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

title: Live television studio work and Ted Nash's soprano date
summary: He worked live TV shows such as The Gong Show; a film date convinced him he did not want the pressure of lead woodwind work.

venues.name: The Tony Orlando and Dawn Show

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Yeah. Records. But a lot of them, my niche, they kind of put you where they want you, and my niche was live television. And so I did all the, well I did part of “The Joey Bishop Show,” “The Della Reese Show,” “The Tony Orlando and Dawn Show,” all the Chuck Barris things, “The Gong Show,” “The $1.98 Beauty Show” “Dinah Shore,” I can’t even think of all of them. But people used to put down live television because sometimes the music was so bad — well no not the music bad, but you just sat around all day long. Like “The Gong Show,” we would rehearse maybe 75 acts, short, and then we would do five shows on Saturday and five shows on Sunday. There was a lot of sitting around because they go so fast you know. Some of those people you know they’d just throw them right off. But see then you get residuals from that. The first re-run is 75%, the next one is a little less and so forth, ad infinitum. So I didn’t see anything wrong. The only trouble is that there is no live television anymore as you can see. Most everything is faded except film. And the guys that got into film and stayed with it are still working, most of them. Film never appealed to me really because I don’t think you can have as much fun with film because it’s too exact. You know some of these people write things like, well I remember I went in to cover a date for Ted Nash, not young Ted but his uncle. Not the Ted Nash in New York, but his uncle, who was a tenor player before him. He became one of the first-call lead players out here, which entails soprano, alto, pic, flute, alto flute, bass flute sometimes, E flat clarinet, B flat clarinet and sometimes bass clarinet. And this date was at the old Columbia picture studio which is on Sunset Boulevard and Gower. © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

And I walked in there and they wanted him to stay to do this one take and he did, and thank God he did it because there was nobody, I mean it was just him all by himself and he started on a high F on soprano, triple piano, just bing. And I realized then, I don’t want to do this. I really don’t have the time to keep that up on those horns to make it my life’s work to do it. And I feel that way today too, I don’t want to do that kind of work. You know you die.
